chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hajjal, from Al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said: I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying:

Good deeds are heavy upon the people of the world in proportion to their weight on their scales on the Day of Resurrection, and bad deeds are light upon the people of the world in proportion to their lightness on their scales on the Day of Resurrection.
ai.seo_question: Why do good deeds feel heavy in this world but are rewarded heavily in the afterlife?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq uses this hadith to illustrate the spiritual paradox of *al-thaqil al-khafif* (the heavy is light), where the discipline required for good deeds makes them feel burdensome in the transient world, yet they carry immense weight in the eternal scales. This reflects the Shia understanding that true ease is found in obedience, while sin offers fleeting lightness at the cost of ultimate significance. The narration serves as a practical reminder to endure the 'weight' of worship and character refinement for greater eschatological reward.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 1-61 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Sa’ed ibn Abdullah quoted on the authority of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, on the authority of Al-Hijal, on the authority of Ala’, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Muslim who saidthat he had heard Aba Ja’far al-Baqir (MGB) say,

“Good deeds are as lofty for the people of the world as they are on their balance of deeds on the Resurrection Day. And bad deeds are as bad for the people of the world as they are on their balance of deeds on the Resurrection Day.”
